e-5214.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse
e-5214.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse $(x-2)^2 + \dfrac{(y-2)^2}{4} = 1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
e-5214.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y = 0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+1 & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =0 \\ x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the point $(2,0).$

Calculate the points where the ellipse $x^2 + 3y^2 - 4x -  6y = 2$ (shown above) intercepts the $x$-axis.
e-5213.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y = 0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x-6y & =2 \\ {x}^{2}+3\cdot {0}^{2}-4x-6\cdot 0 & =2 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =2 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x+4)-4 & =2 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4 & =2 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =6 \\ x-2 & =\pm \sqrt{6} \\ x & =2\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(2-\sqrt{6},0)$ and $(2+\sqrt{6},0).$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse
content.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse $\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(0-3)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{3}+\frac{9}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{3}+1 & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{3} & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =0 \\ x-1 & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(1,0).$

after.problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
after.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{1}{9} & =1 \\ 9(x+1)^{2}+25 & =9\cdot 25 \\ 9(x+1)^{2}+25 & =225 \\ 9(x+1)^{2} & =200 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{200}{9} \\ x+1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{200}{9}} \\ x & =-1\pm \frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}

content.problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{1}{9} & =1 \\ 9(x+1)^{2}+25 & =9\cdot 25 \\ 9(x+1)^{2}+25 & =225 \\ 9(x+1)^{2} & =200 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{200}{9} \\ x+1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{200}{9}} \\ x & =-1\pm \frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the points $(-1-\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3},0)$ and $(-1+\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3},0).$

content.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-7)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(0-7)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{49}{9} & =1 \\ 9(x+3)^{2}+(49\cdot 16) & =9\cdot 16 \\ 9(x+3)^{2}+784 & =144 \\ 9(x+3)^{2} & =-640 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =-\frac{640}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(x+3)^{2}\ge 0$, there is no $x$ such that $(x+3)^{2}=-\frac{640}{9}.$ Therefore, the ellipse has no $x$-intercepts, meaning that it does not intercept the $x$-axis at any point.

after.problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse ${x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+6x+6y=3$  intercepts the $x$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+6x+6y & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+3\cdot {0}^{2}+6x+6\cdot 0 & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+6x & =3 \\ (x+3)^{2}-9 & =3 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =3+9 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =12 \\ x+3 & =\pm 2\sqrt{3} \\ x & =-3\pm 2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(-3-2\sqrt{3},0)$ and $(-3+2\sqrt{3},0).$
